title: 12. Britain in the Second World War and the Labour Settlement

segments.text: Wartime mobilisation and sacrifice directly produced the postwar demand for welfare and reconstruction that carried Labour to power in 1945 — this causal link, not Churchill’s biography, is the topic’s central analytical point.

items.text: The wartime blueprint for postwar social security that shaped Labour’s welfare reforms.
The flagship institution of Attlee’s postwar welfare settlement.
Prepare war leadership and home-front mobilisation separately from postwar reform; evaluate Churchill through cabinet and allied cooperation, not heroic biography.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “How did wartime mobilisation and planning shape the Labour welfare reforms of 1945–48?”
Do not treat Churchill as sole decision-maker; war leadership was cabinet- and alliance-based.
Do not say the welfare state started from nothing in 1945; earlier reforms and wartime planning provided real foundations.
Do not confuse military victory with economic strength; postwar Britain faced severe financial constraints.
Britain declared war on Germany in September 1939 after Germany invaded Poland.
Winston Churchill became prime minister in May 1940 during the crisis created by Germany’s western offensive.
Britain participated in major Allied conferences, including Tehran (1943) and Yalta (1945).
The Labour government elected in 1945 created the National Health Service in 1948 and expanded social security and public ownership.
The direct causal link between wartime sacrifice/planning and the 1945 Labour welfare settlement is the topic’s central point, not a biographical account of Churchill.
Postwar Britain was simultaneously victorious and financially exhausted — both facts are needed to understand the accelerating decolonisation covered in Topic 13.
